clue.text: More work? It would be ideal

definitions.meaning: Sir Thomas More wrote a famous book describing an imaginary perfect island
an imagined perfect society, ideal in every respect

explanation.definitionFit: Thomas More's book gave its name to any imagined perfect place, so both senses meet in one title.

clue.text: Measures how long this publication is

definitions.meaning: a verb: clocks or records the duration of something, as a stopwatch does
the newspaper printing this very crossword

explanation.definitionFit: To record durations is to time things, and the paper carrying the puzzle is the London daily of that name.

clue.text: Depicting characters in play, or art

indicators.note: the letters (characters) of the following words are to be rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone describes how a part in a stage play, or a painting, is depicted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters in' suggests actors in a drama; here it means the letters of PLAY, OR and ART, which are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: A depiction or representation of someone, on stage or canvas, is a rendering of them.

clue.text: Old Roman money is repeatedly turning up here in Italy

parts.note: the as was a bronze coin of ancient Rome

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the doubled letters are read from bottom to top
the word is is to be written out twice in succession

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Ancient coins keep turning up at an Italian archaeological site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning up' reads the doubled piece upwards, as this is a down clue. The printed grid answer is a one-letter slip for the Umbrian town.
explanation.definitionFit: Assisi is a hill town in Umbria, the home of St Francis, so it is a place in Italy.

clue.text: Skilfully holding back confusion in meeting

indicators.note: holding means the word for skilfully keeps the other piece inside it

parts.note: ably means skilfully, competently

indicators.note: back means the word for confusion is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a mess is a state of confusion or disorder

explanation.surface: Someone deftly keeps chaos at bay during a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns the word for confusion around before 'holding' wraps the adverb about it; 'confusion in meeting' tempts a solver to look for a muddle at a gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: A gathering of people for a purpose, such as a school or parliament, is a meeting.

clue.text: One way to be cool if in top-class group

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, written here as AI

indicators.note: in means the word for if goes inside the joined pieces

parts.note: a ring is a group or gang, as of smugglers
an if is a condition, as in 'there's one if'

explanation.surface: A suggestion about staying calm if you're in an exclusive set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' places CONDITION inside AIRING, after AIR. A1 (written AI) is a standard crossword sign for top-class.
explanation.definitionFit: A cooling system for rooms is one means of keeping the temperature down in hot weather.

clue.text: Second drink I have makes me frisky

parts.note: port is a fortified wine from Portugal
contracted to I've

explanation.surface: A drinker boasts that a second glass of port livens them up.
explanation.definitionFit: Sportive means playful and lively, the same high spirits as being frisky.

clue.text: This joined centre of Paris to outskirts, initially

definitions.text: This joined centre of Paris to outskirts, initially

parts.note: met as in came together, connected

indicators.note: the middle letter of the five-letter name Paris is taken
initially means only the opening letter of the word outskirts is used

explanation.surface: A description of the Paris underground linking the city centre to its suburbs.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and description: MET, then R from the centre of Paris, then O from the start of 'outskirts'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Paris underground railway, the Métro, carries passengers between the heart of the city and its suburbs.

clue.text: Ways artist breaks law in ultimate provocation

indicators.note: breaks means the other pieces split the word law open and sit inside

parts.note: taken as written
ways are streets, ST twice for the plural
RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword artist

explanation.surface: A street artist defies the law, which proves the final provocation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaks' signals the container: the streets and the Royal Academician split the word law. 'Ways' gives two street abbreviations because it is plural.
explanation.definitionFit: The final small burden that makes something unbearable is the one that tips patience over the edge.

clue.text: Company director — one involved with Paris and Rome

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: involved means the letters of the two city names are tangled together into a new order

explanation.surface: A theatre producer has dealings with two European capitals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Involved' signals the anagram of the two capitals; 'company' means a theatre or opera troupe, not a business.
explanation.definitionFit: An impresario runs a theatrical or opera company, organising and financing its productions.

clue.text: Job centre in Acton receiving request

indicators.note: the middle letter of the five-letter place name Acton is taken

parts.note: receiving means the central letter takes on the following word beside it

explanation.surface: A Jobcentre in the London district of Acton gets an enquiry.
explanation.walkthrough: Acton is a district of west London; a Jobcentre is a British state employment office, which makes 'Job centre' look like one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A task is a piece of work to be done, the same as a job.

clue.text: Drink produced under pressure swallowed by one's press officer

indicators.note: swallowed by means the letters sit inside the run of words one's press officer

explanation.surface: A drink gulped by a company's media spokesperson.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'onE'S PRESS Officer'.
explanation.definitionFit: Espresso coffee is made by forcing steam or hot water at pressure through ground beans.

clue.text: Extreme changes involved if Maoist turns to this

definitions.text: Extreme changes involved if Maoist turns to this

indicators.note: changes to the outermost letters of the word Maoist rearrange it, the first and last swapping places

explanation.surface: A follower of Mao would need to change radically to adopt a gentle Chinese philosophy.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the first and last letters of MAOIST (M and T) and it becomes the Chinese philosophy; the whole clue also describes that dramatic conversion.
explanation.definitionFit: The Chinese philosophy of the Tao is far from Maoist doctrine, so converting would be a drastic shift.

clue.text: Edward has to be pulled from fast-running river

indicators.note: has to be pulled from means the short name is taken out of the word for fast

parts.note: speedy means fast
Ed is short for Edward

explanation.surface: A man called Edward must be rescued from a rushing torrent.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spey is a fast-flowing Scottish salmon river; taking ED from SPEEDY leaves its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spey is a Scottish salmon-fishing waterway flowing into the Moray Firth.

clue.text: Bill holds city seat

indicators.note: holds means the word for bill contains the name of the city

parts.note: a bill is a poster stuck on a wall
Rio de Janeiro is a Brazilian city

explanation.surface: A legislative bill secures a city a seat in parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holds' signals the container. 'Seat' means the buttocks, not a chair or a constituency.
explanation.definitionFit: Seat in the sense of one's backside, the part of the body one sits on.

clue.text: Drawing instruments, such as rulers?

definitions.meaning: a pair of compasses with two points, used to measure off distances on a drawing
those who divide, as in the maxim divide and rule

explanation.definitionFit: Measuring compasses are named for splitting lengths, and rulers who split their subjects to control them are also splitters.

clue.text: School's head has girl brought in to face expulsion

indicators.note: brought in to means the letters go inside the word for face

parts.note: a dial is a clock face

indicators.note: head means the first letter of the word School's

parts.note: miss is a girl or young woman

explanation.surface: A headteacher brings in a girl to confront her expulsion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought in to' signals the container; 'face' is a clock face, not a verb meaning confront.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sent away from school or a job is a sacking or ejection.

clue.text: Tory politician runs into trouble with dailies

indicators.note: into means the abbreviation goes inside the rearranged letters
trouble means the letters of dailies are stirred up into a new order

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A Conservative MP gets into difficulty with the daily newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouble' shuffles DAILIES and 'into' places R within it.
explanation.definitionFit: Benjamin Disraeli was a Conservative prime minister of the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Religious writer composed missal, in part

indicators.note: in means the rearranged letters sit inside the abbreviation for part
composed means the letters of missal are put together in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A churchman wrote part of a prayer book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composed' signals the anagram and 'in' the container; 'missal' and 'religious writer' make a church scene that hides the mechanics.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer of psalms, such as King David, composed sacred songs.

clue.text: Points made with needles

parts.note: points of the compass: south
points of the compass: east
points of the compass: west
points of the compass: north

explanation.surface: Fine stitches are produced by needlework.
explanation.walkthrough: Four compass points give the letters; 'points' and 'needles' suggest knitting or embroidery.
explanation.definitionFit: Stitched with thread, as fabric is when joined using a needle.

clue.text: Show improvement with respect to criminal record

parts.note: re means concerning, with respect to
form is British slang for a criminal record

explanation.surface: A convict with a record is said to be mending their ways.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a criminal with 'form' has previous convictions.
explanation.definitionFit: To reform is to change for the better, to mend one's ways.

clue.text: African pair of black monarchs

indicators.note: pair of means the black-plus-monarch combination appears twice

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
ER is a monarch, Elizabeth Regina; two of them here

explanation.surface: A pair of African kings dressed in black.
explanation.walkthrough: ER (Elizabeth Regina) is the crossword's standard monarch; B and ER together, doubled.
explanation.definitionFit: The Berbers are an indigenous people of North Africa.

clue.text: Unworthy of English in setback

indicators.note: in means the abbreviation goes inside the word for setback

parts.note: a blow is a setback or misfortune

explanation.surface: Someone thinks the English team's defeat beneath them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Below' in the sense of 'beneath' someone's dignity.
explanation.definitionFit: Something beneath someone's dignity is not good enough for them.

clue.text: A unique ship? That's a joke

parts.note: one of a kind, a single unique thing
a liner is a large passenger ship

explanation.surface: Someone laughs off claims about a one-of-a-kind ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-liner is a brief quip or witticism delivered in a single sentence.

clue.text: Pick hat up and finally leave

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word for hat is read from the bottom

parts.note: tile is old slang for a hat

indicators.note: finally means only the closing letter of the word leave

explanation.surface: Someone gathers up their hat and eventually leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' turns TILE into ELIT, and 'finally' adds E from the end of 'leave'.
explanation.definitionFit: The pick of something is its best part, the select few.

clue.text: River? Hardly!

parts.note: a waterway so small it barely deserves the name of river

explanation.definitionFit: A rill is a tiny brook or trickle, far too slight to count as a proper flowing waterway.

clue.text: Daily post sorted in Irish depot

indicators.note: sorted means the letters of Irish depot are rearranged into order

explanation.surface: A day's mail is processed at a depot in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily post' looks like the mail; it is a job on a daily newspaper. 'Sorted' shuffles IRISH DEPOT.
explanation.definitionFit: The position of running a newspaper, such as a daily, is a senior post.

clue.text: Gunman being exposed in the Sun?

definitions.meaning: John Moses ... was a famous American firearms designer
tanning or turning darker from sunlight

explanation.definitionFit: John Browning designed pistols and machine guns, and skin turning bronze in sunshine is going darker.

clue.text: He pictured peasants in the grass

definitions.meaning: Jean-François ..., French painter of rural labourers such as The Gleaners
a cereal grass grown for its small seeds

explanation.definitionFit: The French painter of The Gleaners shares his name with a cereal crop of the grass family.
